summary: States the IETF's position on building wiretapping capability into IETF standards-track protocols. It explains what the question means, why the answer is no, and what that answer implies. It is an informational statement of policy rather than a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2804 records the IETF's decision not to design wiretapping requirements into its standards. It explains the technical definition used in the memo and the security and jurisdictional reasons for that position.

questions: does the ietf support wiretapping in protocols
what is the raven process ietf
what is the ietf policy on wiretapping
subtitle: The IETF's position on adding wiretapping features to its standards.

tldr.problem: The IETF was asked whether standards-track protocols should include features designed to facilitate wiretapping.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB and IESG define the technical meaning of wiretapping, explain the discussion, and state the IETF's policy and reasons.
tldr.outcome: The IETF decided not to consider wiretapping requirements when creating or maintaining standards, while saying that such mechanisms should be openly described.

today: RFC 2804 is an Informational memo published in May 2000, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the IETF's policy position stated in that memo.

sections.title: The IETF's Policy
sections.content:
The IETF decided not to consider requirements for wiretapping as part of creating or maintaining IETF standards. The memo says laws differ across the jurisdictions where Internet standards are used, making the IETF an unsuitable forum for designing features driven by individual national laws.

The memo also argues that adding wiretapping requirements increases protocol complexity and can weaken security. It restates the IETF's belief that strong cryptographic technology should be widely available, and says mechanisms that facilitate wiretapping should be openly described for review.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF decided not to add wiretapping requirements to its standards. It says such features add complexity and can create security weaknesses.

sections.title: The Raven Discussion
sections.content:
The question arose during IETF work on IP-based telephony. The IETF management arranged a public discussion before deciding whether the working group should proceed with intercept features. A mailing list called Raven was created, followed by discussion at an IETF plenary.

The IESG and IAB were asked to formulate a policy after that discussion. The memo presents this process as background for its position.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy question came up during work on Internet telephony. The IETF discussed it publicly before the IESG and IAB stated a position.

sections.title: The Memo's Definition of Wiretapping
sections.content:
The memo defines wiretapping as deliberately delivering Internet information to a third party without the sender or recipients knowing, when the sender normally expects the information to remain with the intended recipients or parties bound to confidentiality. All four conditions must hold.

The definition excludes monitoring public newsgroups, random monitoring of a large population, and a recipient sharing private email. It includes call-tracing information from accounting logs. The memo describes capture, filtering, and delivery as three steps in the process.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo calls an activity wiretapping when a third party deliberately receives information without the sender or recipients knowing. The sender must also normally expect that information to remain private.

sections.title: The Practical Limits of Wiretapping
sections.content:
The memo observes that copying traffic between users with known points of attachment is not difficult. Linking network locations to people is harder because it involves address assignment, name resolution, and other systems.

It notes that users can take steps to avoid being identified, and that strong encryption can leave recorded traffic unreadable apart from traffic analysis. The memo concludes that Internet wiretapping may be less useful against an alerted and technically capable adversary than expected.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic can be copied, but identifying the people behind it can require information from several systems. Strong encryption can keep message content unavailable to someone who records it.

sections.title: Why a Wiretap Feature Changes Security
sections.content:
The memo says that a system supporting wiretapping must allow information to be released without alerting the sender. Such a system therefore cannot guarantee privacy when the wiretap function might be used.

The added function also makes the system more complex, increasing the risk of unintended security flaws. The RFC concludes that wiretapping lowers system security even when the feature is not being exercised.
sections.plainLanguage: A system that can secretly expose communications cannot guarantee that those communications remain private. Adding that capability also increases system complexity and the chance of security flaws.

references.text: IAB and IESG, "IAB and IESG Statement on Cryptographic Technology and the Internet", RFC 1984, August 1996.
